newsitem.title: CHINA: China central banker sees no need for rate cut.
newsitem.headline: China central banker sees no need for rate cut.

text.p: China does not need to cut interest rates to stimulate its economy in the near term, central bank vice governor Chen Yuan was quoted on Saturday as saying.
Chen said the economy was likely to grow at 9.0-9.5 percent this year, topping the official target of 8.0 percent, the Shanghai Securities News reported.
Premier Li Peng announced the eight percent target in his report to parliament early this year, although government think tanks and economists have put growth between 9.0-10.0 percent.
China cut interest rates twice last year as inflationary pressure eased, and economists as well as industrialists have been pushing for further reductions this year.

Chen said he expected retail price inflation to be about four percent this year, below the official forecast of 6.0 percent. Retail price inflation was 6.1 percent last year, down from a communist-era high of 21.8 percent in 1994.
The annual rate for one-year fixed bank deposits is now 7.47 percent, down from 9.15 percent in May 1996.
Economists have argued that further interest rate reductions would take some financial pressure off cash-strapped state firms, which are saddled with heavy debt burdens.
But the central bank has been concerned that a cut in interest rates would slow the growth of bank savings deposits.

That could also mean more cash would enter the already volatile stock market, which central authorities are trying to rein in, and hamper efforts to sell treasury bonds needed to meet state budget targets.
Chen was also quoted as saying there was upward pressure on the nation's currency, the yuan, but the local unit was now at an appropriate level.
He said the central bank would keep the yuan stable. It stood at 8.2905 to the dollar in Shanghai on Friday.
